record.paper_title: Open problems in the theory of completely positive and copositive matrices
record.original_question: Does the Drew-Johnson-Loewy bound hold for n = 6? Equivalently, if p_n = max{cpr(A) : A is in CP_n} and cpr(A) is the minimum number of columns in a nonnegative B with A = B B^T, is p_6 equal to floor(6^2/4) = 9?

evidence.quote: as is the question whether the DJL conjecture holds for n = 6.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A real symmetric matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is called completely positive if there exists an entrywise nonnegative matrix $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ (for some integer $k \geq 1$) such that $A = BB^T$. Let $\mathrm{CP}_n$ denote the cone of all $n \times n$ completely positive matrices. For $A \in \mathrm{CP}_n$, the cp-rank of $A$, denoted $\mathrm{cpr}(A)$, is the smallest integer $k$ for which such a nonnegative factor $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ exists. Define
$$p_n \;=\; \max\{\mathrm{cpr}(A) : A \in \mathrm{CP}_n\}.$$
The Drew–Johnson–Loewy conjecture asserts that for every integer $n \geq 4$,
$$p_n \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4} \right\rfloor.$$
Determine whether this equality holds in the case $n = 6$; that is, decide whether $p_6 = \lfloor 36/4 \rfloor = 9$.
artifact.status_search_result: The Drew–Johnson–Loewy conjecture has been proved for n=5 and disproved for all n≥7 (counterexamples by Bomze–Schachinger–Ullrich), but the n=6 case remains open. Partial progress shows the bound cpr(A) ≤ 9 holds for 6×6 completely positive matrices orthogonal to an exceptional extremal copositive matrix, but no full resolution is known.

status_evidence.title: On the DJL conjecture for order 6
status_evidence.snippet: Recently this conjecture has been proved for n=5 and disproved for n≥7, leaving the case n=6 open.
status_evidence.claim: The n=6 case of the DJL conjecture is explicitly stated as still open.
